title: Empower clients and communities to make sound scientific decisions

lessons.title: What a sound scientific decision is
lessons.html:
From telling to empowering

Traditional extension often told farmers what to do. Empowerment means building farmers' ability to make good decisions themselves, using evidence, sound reasoning and their own knowledge. An empowered farmer can judge a new seed variety, a feed supplement or a salesperson's claim without waiting for an extension officer.

Features of a sound scientific decision

  • Based on evidence: facts from trials, records, measurements and reliable sources rather than rumour or advertising alone.
  • Considers the whole system: soil, water, animals, labour, cash flow and markets.
  • Weighs costs, benefits and risks, in rands and in risk to the household.
  • Tested where possible: tried on a small scale before full use.
  • Reviewed: checked afterwards to learn whether it worked.

Common decision traps

  • Believing a product works because a neighbour said so once, or because the label looks impressive.
  • Judging from one good or bad season, which may simply reflect rainfall.
  • Comparing fields or herds that differ in soil, management or age, so the comparison is unfair.
  • Ignoring costs: a higher yield is not a gain if input costs rise more than income.

Combining science with local knowledge

Farmers already observe carefully. They know which camp floods, which cows calve easily, which soils hold water. Scientific thinking adds structure: clear questions, fair comparisons, measurement and records. Respect what farmers know and help them test and strengthen it.

An example: a group of maize growers in Mpumalanga wants to know whether a new hybrid suits their area. Instead of telling them, the extensionist helps them set up a fair comparison on several farms, measure yields and calculate the return per rand spent. The group then decides, and understands why.

lessons.title: Tools for evidence-based decisions
lessons.html:
Teaching farmers to gather and use evidence

Farmer-managed trials

A simple on-farm trial compares two or more options under the same conditions.

  1. Ask a clear question, for example: does lime increase our maize yield on these acid soils?
  2. Choose plots that are as similar as possible.
  3. Change only one thing; keep everything else the same.
  4. Repeat the comparison on several farms or plots so that results are not due to chance.
  5. Measure the result, such as yield in kg per plot.
  6. Calculate costs and returns.

Soil and other tests

A soil analysis from an accredited laboratory shows pH and nutrient levels, so fertiliser and lime decisions are based on facts rather than guesswork. Teach farmers how to take a representative sample and how to read the main results with your help. Similar evidence comes from water tests, faecal egg counts for worms in sheep and goats, and pregnancy diagnosis in cattle.

Records

Records are the farmer's own evidence. Simple records of rainfall, planting dates, inputs, yields, births, deaths, sales and costs allow farmers to compare seasons and spot problems. Even a notebook or a phone app is enough.

Simple economic analysis

Extra cost per haR0R1 200

Value of extra yield at R3 500 per tR0R2 100
Net gain per haR0R900

These figures are an example only. Use the farmer's own prices and results. Help farmers also ask what happens in a dry year, because a practice that pays only in good years may be too risky.

Judging information sources

Teach farmers to ask: who is giving this information, what do they gain, is there evidence from trials, and has it worked under conditions like mine?

lessons.title: Facilitating community decision making
lessons.html:
Empowering groups and communities

Many important decisions are collective: how to manage communal grazing, whether to invest in a shared borehole, which crops a cooperative should grow for a contract. The extensionist's role is to help the community make an informed, well-reasoned decision, not to make it for them.

A decision-making process for communities

  1. Clarify the decision and who it affects.
  2. Gather evidence: veld condition assessments, water availability, market information, trial results, expert input from researchers or the state veterinarian.
  3. Present information clearly: use local language, pictures, maps and simple numbers.
  4. Identify options and their consequences, including environmental effects and effects on different groups such as women, youth and households with few animals.
  5. Deliberate: allow enough time for discussion, including in traditional structures.
  6. Decide and record the decision and reasons.
  7. Monitor and review outcomes together.

Respecting legal and environmental limits

Some decisions are bounded by law. For example, overgrazing and cultivation of erodible land are regulated under the Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983, and water use is regulated under the National Water Act 36 of 1998. Explain these limits honestly so that the community can choose among lawful options.

Your ethical responsibilities

  • Present balanced information, including uncertainties and risks.
  • Declare when you are unsure and refer to specialists.
  • Do not favour a supplier, buyer or programme because it benefits you.
  • Respect the community's right to decide, even when you would choose differently, unless the decision is unlawful or unsafe.

Building lasting capacity

Each decision is a learning opportunity. Review it afterwards: what evidence was most useful, what was missing, what would we do differently? Over time the community develops its own habit of evidence-based decision making.

Key points

  • Empowerment builds farmers' own ability to decide using evidence.
  • Sound decisions use evidence, consider the whole system and weigh costs and risks.
  • Fair on-farm trials change only one thing and are repeated.
  • Records, soil tests and simple economic analysis are key tools.
  • Present balanced information and respect the community's right to decide.
